newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey says to cut wheat import tax if prices rise.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says to cut wheat import tax if prices rise.

text.p: Turkey is considering a reduction in customs tax on wheat imports only if local wheat prices rise again, a senior grain official said on Wednesday.
"The tax will be reduced if the prices get out of control and rise again," the official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.

His comments came a few hours after Agriculture Minister Musa Demirci told a news conference that the tax could be lowered to three percent from the present 15 to make imports cheaper for the grain board (TMO) and private millers.
"To reduce the cost of imports the tax could be lowered to three percent. We are working on it," Demirci said.
But the grain official said "If prices rise to levels they were at last week, then the tax reduction will be considered."
"Local wheat prices are now at the desired level. The TMO sells at 23,000 lira (per kg), which is the average price in the market," he said.

Per kilo prices of milling wheat surged by about 30 percent to 27,000 lira three weeks ago, when Turkey began stringent inspections on imported U.S. wheat against ergot fungus, leading to a U.S. government suspension of grain export certificates to Turkey.

Turkey was enforcing a zero-tolerance limit for ergot fungus in its Food Quarantine Act, but later backed down by raising the limit to first 0.02 percent and then to 0.05 percent after criticism from millers and U.S. officials.
But prices declined to 23,000 lira after the TMO decided last week to sell milling wheat locally from its stocks of about 700,000 tonnes.
Demirci indicated on Tuesday the TMO might import an unspecified amount of milling wheat in December.
The TMO has been authorised by the government to import up to 500,000 tonnes to curb rising local wheat and bread prices, but no date for the imports has been given.
Asked when and how much the import would be, Demirci said: "We will import whenever necessary and at the required amount."
Traders said the TMO would have to import some wheat soon to control the price of bread, a staple for millions of Turks.
"The tax reduction will come, sooner or later, and they (TMO) will have to import wheat," said a Turkey-based trader from an international company.
"We feel the decree (on tax reduction) has to come because millers cannot reduce local flour prices unless they produce flour with cheaper wheat," he said.
Millers, who depend largely on imported wheat to produce flour for export and domestic consumption, said the quality of local wheat was questionable and imports were inevitable.

Erdem Ozkasikci, head of Turkey's Millers' Association, said their profit margins did not allow them to sell flour at 1.45 million lira per sack (50 kg), the level at which the government demanded they sell last week to reduce bread prices.
"The current price of a sack of flour is 1.9 million and we cannot go lower than that," he said.
"The 15-percent import tax should be reduced if they want us to sell flour at cheaper levels," he said.
Turkey has imported about 1.5 million tonnes of wheat so far in 1996 and the government has granted import licences for 3.2 million tonnes for imports until the end of this year.
Demirci said no U.S. wheat was being held at any port in Turkey and there was no intention of a crackdown on U.S. wheat.
"Any food item from the United States can enter Turkey as long as they meet the quality standards," he said. "We have never banned imports from the United States."
--Ercan Ersoy, Ankara Newsroom, 90-312-4462940
